thread.title: The tax bill isn't all free money The overarching consensus

author: Paulo Santos
title: The tax bill isn't all free money The overarching consensus
text:
The tax bill isn't all free money 
The overarching consensus when it comes to the Trump tax bill and its stock market consequence is that it’s a massive positive that’s responsible for a large increase in the stock market’s value.
This is mostly centered on the headline tax corporate tax rate falling all the way from 35% to 21%. A 14% drop on 65% (100%-35%) of net profits could conceivably add as much as 21.5% to the market’s value, if it translated into such an increase in headline EPS.
In this article, though, I’ll show that there are endless caveats and unexpected consequences, which greatly reduce this impact. So let’s see.
The Tax Bill Is A Domestic (US) Tax Bill That is, the drop in headline tax rates ultimately applies to profits made in the US. As it turns out, the largest capitalizations in the market sell a large part of their wares abroad. For instance:
S&P 500 companies had 43.2% of their 2016 sales in foreign countries. And this was actually a depressed share due to USD strength. Back in 2014 these were 47.4% and right now they ought to be trending there again due to USD weakness. Within the S&P, information and technology, which would be a proxy for the typical Nasdaq security, had 57.1% of its 2016 sales in foreign lands. This was closer to 60% in 2014, and should be heading there again with USD weakness. As a result of this geographical distribution, right from the bat a large share of profits will take place in foreign lands. Also as a result, it won’t actually benefit from the large drop in UA corporate tax rates. If we use “half” as a good measure, this would mean only half of the profits would be exposed to the 14% drop in tax rates. Immediately, the possible impact on earnings would plunge to 10.75% from the previously stated 21.5%.
A caveat here. The US tax rate supposedly applies to earnings anywhere in the world. However, it gets deferred for earnings abroad until they were actually brought back into the US – which they mostly never were, so we can dismiss this formal notion and stick the practical notion that only US earnings were taxed at US rates.
Tax Optimization Being able to earn profits abroad opened another can of worms: Tax optimization. Transfer pricing. Patent and trademark location. A thousand other schemes allowed large corporations to place earnings where they’d be taxed the least.
This included squeezing profits out of the US and into those foreign jurisdictions, even beyond the actual share of sales. Hence me considering “half” above. The result of this (and other domestic tax deductions) is that the actual average effective federal tax rate in the US was ~20%, if we consider corporate tax receipts and pretax corporate income .
Given that the effective tax rate was already much lower than the headline tax rate, it immediately becomes obvious that the upside to a lower headline tax rate cannot be as large as it seems. Moreover, the tax bill imposes minimum foreign taxes on foreign income at a rate of 10.5%. Foreign taxes already paid on foreign profits are 80% deducted from this amount, so this kind of imposes a minimum 13.125% foreign tax. Either way, 10.5% on foreign income becomes the bare minimum.
Including both, this would thus mean that 21% x 50% (of income) + 10.5% x 50% = 15.75% would become a kind of floor for actual effective federal income tax rates. The heavy capex deductions could help and take it lower still, though. But from here it would already seem that:
The maximum overall gain would be under 5% of the actual effective rates. Thus 5% / 80% = ~ 6.25% impact on actual market-wide earnings , instead of the 21.5% first computed or the 10.75% coming straight from there being a foreign component to earnings. For companies with already-existing very low effective tax rates, the gains could be smaller or even not exist at all. Here, two curiosities:
IBM ( IBM ) recently guided its FY2018 effective tax rate to 14%-18%, from and adjusted 12% during FY2017. Thus, IBM - which is starting from a very low effective tax rate - will actually see a higher tax rate going forward. Intel ( INTC ) recently guided its 2018 effective tax rate to 14%. This is down from 22.5% in 2017 and 20.3% in 2016. Intel is a heavy gainer from capex deductions as it acts in a capex-intensive industry. Still, its gains are 6.3%-8.5%, still far from the 14% drop on headline corporate tax rate. While there will be wild variation from company to company, what this highlights is that the actual gains from the tax rate drop are significantly smaller than what the headline tax rate would make you believe. But it doesn’t stop here.
One-Off Tax On Accumulated Foreign Income As we saw previously, US corporate tax rates were already supposed to apply to worldwide income. However, as long as profits stayed abroad, the tax on them was indefinitely postponed (deferred).
Now, that changes. There will no longer be any tax on repatriation of profits. However, past accumulated foreign profits will be subjected to a 15.5% tax (on liquid assets) or 8% (on illiquid assets). This mostly trends toward 15.5%. This one-off tax applies on the full amounts whether companies elect to repatriate assets or not . I’m highlighting this because at times there seem to be confusion where media talks as if it could be less if a company wanted to repatriate less cash. It couldn’t.
This tax can lead to a significant upfront cost. For instance, Apple ( AAPL ), which will pay the largest amount for sure, is talking about $38 billion. $38 billion is 59.3% of Apple’s entire FY2017 pretax profit . Apple had an effective tax rate of 24.6% on those pretax profits.
Now, if we consider Apple might lower its effective tax rate by, say, 6%, what would that mean? It would mean that the first 9.9 years in tax rate reduction would be paid for, upfront . Then one has to ask, where will tax rates be in the next 9.9 years? It’s not even a certainty that Apple would come out ahead on this deal, though one tends to project tax rates into eternity at the present levels.
Apple is just an example. The same logic applies to most other large multinationals with similar results . Some will be paying fewer years upfront, others will be paying more years upfront. IBM will be paying infinite years upfront, since it gets both a tax bill and no tax savings.
Who most obviously gains? Those companies whose profits are generated nearly all in the US and don’t have large foreign tax deferred assets . They get the tax savings and don’t get the one-off tax bill. Regional banks, retailers, etc., are most often within this segment.
The Buyback Bonanza As a result of the removal of taxing on repatriation, there’s the thesis swirling around in the market that all that foreign cash will lead to a buyback bonanza. Companies will bring in their massive cash hoards and spend it buying back stock.
There are, however, two large impediments to this:
The first is that most of the largest companies, including Apple, Microsoft ( MSFT ) and many others, had already been buying back stock hand over fist even without bringing in the foreign money. For that, they took on debt. A lot of debt. For instance, Apple has $115.7 billion of financial debt on its books. It also has $268.9 billion in cash and financial assets, but the debt shows just how large the buybacks it’s pursuing already are. During FY2017 Apple bought back $33 billion of its own stock and also paid $12.8 billion in dividends. Apple’s investor returns combining those two fractions were already at $45.8 billion – that’s not far from the $51.1 billion it made from operating cash flow minus capex. There isn’t much room to continue increasing it (unless operating cash flow increases further in a sustainable fashion). The second is that the one-off tax bill already takes a large (though one-off) slice of the cash available for repurchase of stock. For instance, when it comes to Apple it removes 24.8% of its net cash . Will Apple be moved to increase buybacks substantially when it sees 24.8% of net cash evaporate and is already returning cash at levels near the free cash flow it produces? Unlikely. Apple could (and likely will) make a token increase in buybacks and dividends, but is unlikely to move toward a large increase. The same logic applies over and over. In places, like IBM, one could even argue that buybacks ought to be curtailed. A buyback bonanza from large, international, companies looks unlikely. Those are the ones which dominate the S&P 500 and Nasdaq. The smaller, domestic-only players might have room for more buybacks, though.
On Valuation We’ve already seen that the overall impact on earnings from lower taxes is likely not to be massive. Certainly, it is likely to be very far from the 21.5% which could be implied from the cut in headline tax rates. It could be around 6-7%, all things considered. So for a given price, the market’s price/earnings would become roughly 6-7% cheaper.
However, an odd thing happens here. There are multiples which don’t become cheaper because of the tax bill. Indeed, they can become more expensive. Consider the following:
EV/EBITDA . EBITDA doesn’t move on tax rates. However, EV subtracts cash. Cash will take a hit from the one-off repatriation tax, a hit we saw could be as large as nearly one-fourth of Apple’s net cash. As a result of this, in overall EV/EBITDA terms the market will become slightly more expensive due to the tax bill, reflecting the one-off upfront cash payments. We’re in an already historically expensive market when it comes to EV/EBITDA, too. Price/Book Value . Price/book doesn’t improve on lower tax rates. However, companies which accumulated large NOLs (Net Operating Losses) will see these take a large hit because if they get profits to use the NOLs on, those profits would be taxed lower. Moreover, use of NOLs going forward also is more restricted, further reducing their value. A charge due to NOLs losing value will reduce book value in unprofitable companies (both those unprofitable in the present, and those which were unprofitable for long stretches in the past and still have large NOLs). In addition, the one-off repatriation tax also will affect book value in profitable companies whose profits were held abroad. The net result is that there’s an impact to book value and thus the market is likely to become ever so slightly more expensive even without the price moving. Of note here, some of the book charges can be ignored in most businesses, but maybe not in businesses which rely on regulatory capital thresholds (insurers, fintech, banks, etc). There, booking large charges, even if non-cash, can lead to the companies having to take (negative) action when it comes to dividend-paying activity, buyback activity or even create the need to raise capital.
Conclusion Given the many moving parts, the tax bill effect isn’t nearly as positive as the market seems to think it is. The overall impact is likely around 6-7% or so of the market’s valuation, from an earnings perspective, and varies significantly from company to company. It’s more than likely this impact has long been priced in.
Moreover, even that impact is in large measure paid for upfront due to the one-time repatriation tax. It might be that the upfront payment for many multinational companies is so large that in a few years, if tax policy changes again, it would make the current lower taxes a losing proposition. However, the market does tend to ignore these one-off items and concentrate on the “ongoing improvement” (lower taxes).
Finally, and somewhat surprisingly, there are valuation measures (EV/EBITDA, Price/Book) which will even look slightly more expensive because of the tax bill. The reason here is mostly due to the upfront charges (cash or non-cash) which those measures actually take into account.
